jubilee.what: One person with a strong view sits in the middle of 20 people who disagree, and anyone can take the chair to argue.
Two groups on opposite sides of an issue try to find what they actually agree on.
People who share one identity show how differently they think about it, stepping forward on statements.

skills.name: Steelmanning
skills.idea: Put the other side's argument in its strongest form before you answer it. If they would say 'yes, that's exactly what I mean', you have earned the right to disagree.
skills.watchFor: Does anyone restate the other person's point fairly before attacking it?
skills.tryIt: Pick one view you disagree with and say its best version in one sentence.

skills.name: The scout mindset
skills.idea: A soldier defends a position; a scout wants an accurate map, even if it shows they were wrong. Good debaters are scouts first.
skills.watchFor: Who seems curious, and who only seems to want to win?
skills.tryIt: Notice one belief you hold mostly because people around you hold it.
skills.video: Julia Galef why you think you're right even if you're wrong TED

skills.name: Disagreeing productively
skills.idea: Find the shared goal first, then argue about how to get there. It turns 'you versus me' into 'us versus the problem'.
skills.watchFor: Moments where both sides find common ground, even briefly.
skills.tryIt: For one argument you watch, name the goal both sides share.
skills.video: Julia Dhar how to disagree productively TED

skills.name: Empathy is not endorsement
skills.idea: You can understand why someone believes something without agreeing with it. Understanding makes your reply better aimed.
skills.watchFor: Questions that come from curiosity rather than a trap.
skills.tryIt: Ask yourself what experience might lead a reasonable person to the other view.
skills.video: Dylan Marron empathy is not endorsement TED

skills.name: Socratic questions
skills.idea: Instead of stating your view, ask questions that help the other person test theirs. 'How did you come to that?' and 'How sure are you, out of ten?' do more than a speech.
skills.watchFor: Which questions actually make someone pause and think?
skills.tryIt: Write one open question you would ask the person in the chair.

skills.name: Facts versus values
skills.idea: Many arguments mix up what is true with what matters. Two people can agree on every fact and still disagree because they weigh things differently.
skills.watchFor: When the argument is really about values, not evidence.
skills.tryIt: Split one claim you hear into its fact part and its value part.

skills.name: Moral foundations
skills.idea: Jonathan Haidt argues that liberals and conservatives draw on different moral instincts: care and fairness on one side, plus loyalty, authority and sanctity on the other.
skills.watchFor: Which moral instinct each speaker appeals to.
skills.tryIt: Reframe one argument using a value the other side cares about.
skills.video: Jonathan Haidt moral roots of liberals and conservatives TED

skills.name: Spotting a straw man
skills.idea: A straw man is a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument, set up because it is easier to knock down.
skills.watchFor: 'So what you're saying is...' followed by something they did not say.
skills.tryIt: When you hear a summary of someone's view, check it against what they actually said.

skills.name: Ad hominem
skills.idea: Attacking the person instead of the argument. Who someone is does not decide whether their point is right.
skills.watchFor: Comments about age, looks, background or motives instead of the point.
skills.tryIt: Notice how the room reacts to a personal attack. Does it win or lose people?

skills.name: Whataboutism
skills.idea: Answering a criticism with 'what about when your side did X?'. It may be true, but it dodges the original question.
skills.watchFor: A question being met with a different question about the other side.
skills.tryIt: When it happens, ask: was the first point ever answered?

skills.name: False choices
skills.idea: Presenting only two options when more exist: 'either you support this or you hate the country'.
skills.watchFor: 'Either... or' framing, and who quietly offers a third option.
skills.tryIt: For one either/or claim, think of a third option.

skills.name: Moving the goalposts
skills.idea: When evidence is given, the person changes what would count as proof. It means no answer can ever be enough.
skills.watchFor: 'Well, that doesn't count because...' after a fair answer.
skills.tryIt: Before you argue, ask: what evidence would change your mind?

skills.name: The Gish gallop
skills.idea: Throwing out lots of quick claims so the other person cannot answer them all. Volume can look like strength.
skills.watchFor: Fast lists of claims, and whether anyone picks just one to examine properly.
skills.tryIt: If you are flooded with points, choose the strongest one and focus there.

skills.name: Stories versus data
skills.idea: A powerful personal story can be true and still not represent the bigger picture. Good arguments use both stories and numbers.
skills.watchFor: Which persuades the room more: a story or a statistic?
skills.tryIt: Ask of one story you hear: how typical is this?

skills.name: Define your terms
skills.idea: Many arguments fall apart because people mean different things by the same word, like 'freedom', 'woke' or 'fair'.
skills.watchFor: A key word both sides use differently.
skills.tryIt: Pick one loaded word and write your own one-line definition.
skills.video: define your terms in an argument

skills.name: Point, reason, example, point
skills.idea: A simple structure for speaking clearly: say your point, give one reason, back it with an example, then repeat the point.
skills.watchFor: Who is easy to follow, and what structure they use.
skills.tryIt: Make one argument out loud using PREP, in under 30 seconds.

skills.name: Listening properly
skills.idea: Most people listen to reply, not to understand. Short questions and letting silence sit make people say more.
skills.watchFor: Who interrupts, and who lets the other person finish.
skills.tryIt: In your next conversation, ask one follow-up question before giving your view.
skills.video: Celeste Headlee 10 ways to have a better conversation TED

skills.name: Conceding a point
skills.idea: Admitting 'that's a fair point' when it is builds trust and makes your other points land harder.
skills.watchFor: Does anyone concede anything? How does the room respond?
skills.tryIt: Find one point from the other side you can honestly agree with.
skills.video: how to concede a point in a debate

skills.name: Staying calm
skills.idea: Calm reads as confidence. Slowing down, lowering your voice and pausing before answering helps you think and keeps the other person listening.
skills.watchFor: Who gets louder, and whether it helps them.
skills.tryIt: Take one slow breath before replying in your next disagreement.
skills.video: how to stay calm in an argument
